label: Anger at God
framing: You are allowed to be angry at God. Scripture is full of believers who brought their rage straight to him rather than away from him, and the surprising thing is that he does not strike them down for it; he stays in the room. Anger at God is often faith refusing to let go of a God it can no longer understand.
cultural: Our culture treats anger at God as either blasphemy to be suppressed or proof that God is not worth believing in, and so it leaves the wounded believer with nowhere to take the protest. The Bible refuses both exits. It gives the sufferer a language of lament, an honest, accusing, unresolved speech directed at God, and it counts that speech as a form of prayer, not a departure from it.
historical: Job in his ash heap accused God to his face for thirty chapters. When God answered, he met Job with hard questions out of the whirlwind (Job 38:2), yet it was the comforters, who had defended God, whom he said had not spoken accurately about him, as his servant Job had (Job 42:7). The Psalmist cried how long, O Lord, will you forget me forever. Jesus himself, on the cross, prayed the opening line of Psalm 22, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, taking the protest of the abandoned and making it his own. The church has prayed those words ever since.
application: Say the anger out loud to God, in the very words you are afraid to use, because the alternative is not reverence but distance. Read the laments and pray them when your own speech fails. Refuse the false comforters who rush to defend God or explain your suffering, and find instead the friends who will sit in the ash heap with you. And hold on, even angry, since the one who stays in the argument is closer to God than the one who walks away polite.

verses.text: My God, my God, why have You forsaken me? Why are You so far from saving me, so far from my words of groaning? I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer, and by night, but I have no rest.
verses.where: The psalm opens with the most famous cry of dereliction in Scripture. The site's note says the sufferer still calls God his own; he asks why his God has left him, by day and by night, and keeps praying through the silence. Its plain note says that if a man can pray these words and still be a man of faith, so can you.

verses.text: At the ninth hour, Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
verses.where: After three hours of darkness Jesus cries out from the cross in the opening words of Psalm 22, and in Mark they are the last words he says. The site's note says this gives every sufferer who has asked why a place to stand within faith, since the Son himself asked it and was not rebuked. Even in the cry, he still calls God his God.

verses.text: “Even today my complaint is bitter. His hand is heavy despite my groaning. If only I knew where to find Him, so that I could go to His seat. I would plead my case before Him and fill my mouth with arguments.
verses.where: Job, who has lost his children, his wealth and his health, says his complaint is still bitter, and longs to find God and argue his case to his face. The site's note says the two main ways of reading the passage agree that Scripture takes the experience of God's absence seriously, and that the right response is not to deny it but to bring it to God, as Job does.

verses.text: After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz the Temanite, “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has.
verses.where: Job has just admitted, having seen God, that he spoke of things he did not understand. Then God turns to the friends who spent the long debate defending him and accusing Job, and says they have not spoken of him accurately, as his servant Job has. The book lets God correct Job's understanding and still rebuke the friends who defended him with wrong words.

verses.text: So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble upon this people? Is this why You sent me? Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not delivered Your people in any way.”
verses.where: Moses has obeyed, and things have only grown worse: the slaves must find their own straw and the foremen have been beaten. Moses takes the accusation straight to God, asking why he has brought trouble on his people. The site's note says Scripture records the complaint without rebuke, and God answers not with a reprimand but with a renewed promise.

verses.text: “Do not call me Naomi,” she replied. “Call me Mara, because the Almighty has dealt quite bitterly with me. I went away full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi? After all, the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has afflicted me.”
verses.where: Naomi comes home to Bethlehem having lost her husband and both her sons, and tells the town to call her Mara, bitter, because the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. The site's plain note says the book does not rebuke her or hurry her out of her grief; it answers her slowly, through what happens next. And Ruth is standing beside her as she says it.

verses.text: How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear, or cry out to You, “Violence!” but You do not save? Why do You make me see iniquity? Why do You tolerate wrongdoing? Destruction and violence are before me. Strife is ongoing, and conflict abounds.
verses.where: Habakkuk asks God how long he must cry for help against violence and injustice while God does not seem to hear or save. God's reply in the next chapter calls for faith and patience rather than giving a full explanation. The site's note says what the chapter refuses is the easy answer that God does not care or is not in control.

verses.text: “Will the Lord spurn us forever and never show His favor again? Is His loving devotion gone forever? Has His promise failed for all time? Has God forgotten to be gracious? Has His anger shut off His compassion?” Selah
verses.where: A sleepless psalmist who cannot be comforted asks whether the Lord has rejected his people forever and whether his loving devotion is gone. The site's plain note says you may pray these questions as your own: they are in the Bible, and they were prayed by a temple singer. He keeps talking to God through the night, and then resolves to remember what God has done.

verses.text: When Mary came to Jesus and saw Him, she fell at His feet and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.
verses.where: Mary falls at Jesus' feet and repeats her sister's words exactly: if you had been here, my brother would not have died. The site's note says the repetition suggests the sisters had said it to each other many times in four days of waiting, and that Jesus answers her not with teaching but with his own grief. He does not defend himself; he is deeply moved and troubled.

verses.text: Yet I call this to mind, and therefore I have hope: Because of the loving devotion of the LORD we are not consumed, for His mercies never fail. They are new every morning; great is Your faithfulness!
verses.where: The speaker has described his affliction in the starkest images, God as a bear, a lion, an archer and a jailer who shuts out his prayer. Then he calls to mind the LORD's loving devotion and mercies that are new every morning. The site's note says the chapter does not solve the tension but lives inside it, and that its hope is chosen rather than felt.

misread.taken: “My thoughts are not your thoughts” is quoted to people who ask God why, as if the verse meant that God's ways are a mystery and the questions should stop.
misread.says: The site's note says these verses are sometimes used to shut down hard questions, and that the context points elsewhere. The contrast comes right after verse 7, where the wicked are told that God will freely pardon: his thoughts are higher than ours especially in his readiness to forgive. The same passage says his word comes down like rain and accomplishes his purpose, so he makes himself known. The verses invite humility, not silence.
misread.text: “For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,” declares the LORD. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.

whole: If your anger at God has come with a loss that feels too heavy to live with, or with thoughts of hurting yourself, tell someone you trust today; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Anger at God usually arrives with a name and a date attached: a child who died, a diagnosis, a marriage that ended though you prayed every night, years of asking for one thing and hearing nothing. Some people are angry and frightened of their anger at once, as if God might strike them for it. Some have stopped praying because the only words left feel too harsh to say in church. Some were told that questioning God is a sin, and so they went quiet, and the quiet has become distance.

Scripture keeps the words people are afraid to say. Job demanded a hearing. Moses asked God why he had brought trouble on his people. Naomi told her town that the Almighty had dealt bitterly with her. Habakkuk asked how long he must cry for help, a psalmist asked whether God's love was gone forever, and Jesus himself cried the first line of Psalm 22 from the cross. God does not turn any of them away for speaking. He answers Job out of the whirlwind with hard questions of his own, and still, at the end, it is the friends who defended him with wrong words whom he says have not spoken of him accurately. That does not make every angry word true; Job, having seen God, admits he spoke of things he did not understand. But anger at God is often faith that will not let go. It is addressed to someone, because it still believes he is there, and the site's note on Psalm 13 calls it faith arguing with God.

So the wisdom of Scripture is to take the anger to God rather than away from him. Say it in plain words, the ones you are afraid to use, and when you have none, pray the laments, which were kept for exactly this. Be slow to trust anyone who hurries to defend God by explaining your loss, and look for the friends who will sit with you, as Job's friends did for seven days before they began to talk. Remember what God has done, for others and for you, not to cancel the pain but, as the note on Psalm 22 says, to give it somewhere to go. And expect it to take time. Lament in the Bible rarely resolves in one prayer, and some of its prayers do not resolve at all.

The deepest answer Scripture gives is not an explanation but a person. The God you are angry at did not stay out of reach of the question. In Jesus he cried it himself, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”, and the psalm he prayed ends in praise that widens to a people not yet born. Lamentations finds mercies new every morning in the middle of a chapter that never stops being honest. Hope here is chosen before it is felt, and the one who keeps arguing with God is still talking to him.
deep.sit: What is the sentence you have been afraid to say to God, and what would it be like to say it to him tonight, the way Job and the psalmists did?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says Psalm 13 gives you permission to ask God how long, four times over. Pray all six verses, and if you cannot yet say verse 5 for yourself, say it as the church's words and let them wait in you until they become your own.
prayer.text: How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me? Consider me and respond, O LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, lest I sleep in death, lest my enemy say, “I have overcome him,” and my foes rejoice when I fall. But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.

careLines.text: If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor.
You do not have to carry it alone.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
